claim: Axin1 is a key regulator of canonical Wnt signaling pathway.
source: Axin1 is a key regulator of canonical Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background knowledge about Axin1's function.

claim: Specific deletion of Axin1 in limb mesenchymal cells leads to fibular hemimelia (FH)-like phenotype.
source: Specific deletion of Axin1 in limb mesenchymal cells leads to fibular hemimelia (FH)-like phenotype, associated with tarsal coalition.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: FH disease in Axin1 knockout mice is associated with tarsal coalition.
source: Specific deletion of Axin1 in limb mesenchymal cells leads to fibular hemimelia (FH)-like phenotype, associated with tarsal coalition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations.

claim: FH disease is associated with decreased osteoclast formation in Axin1 knockout mice.
source: Further studies demonstrate that FH disease is associated with additional defects in Axin1 knockout (KO) mice, including decreased osteoclast formation and defects in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from further studies.

claim: FH disease is associated with defects in angiogenesis in Axin1 knockout mice.
source: Further studies demonstrate that FH disease is associated with additional defects in Axin1 knockout (KO) mice, including decreased osteoclast formation and defects in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from further studies.

claim: Axin1 controls limb development through both canonical β-catenin and BMP signaling pathways.
source: We then provide in vivo evidence showing that Axin1 controls limb development through both canonical β-catenin and BMP signaling pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from in vivo evidence.

claim: Inhibition of β-catenin signaling could significantly reverse the FH phenotype in mice.
source: We demonstrate that inhibition of β-catenin or BMP signaling could significantly reverse the FH phenotype in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of BMP signaling could significantly reverse the FH phenotype in mice.
source: We demonstrate that inhibition of β-catenin or BMP signaling could significantly reverse the FH phenotype in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Integration of β-catenin and BMP signaling by Axin1 is required for lower limb development.
source: Together, our findings reveal that integration of β-catenin and BMP signaling by Axin1 is required for lower limb development.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the findings.

claim: Defect in Axin1 signaling could lead to the development of FH disease.
source: Defect in Axin1 signaling could lead to the development of FH disease.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Fibular hemimelia (FH) is a congenital longitudinal limb deficiency characterized by complete or partial absence of the fibular bone.
source: Fibular hemimelia (FH) is a congenital longitudinal limb deficiency characterized by complete or partial absence of the fibular bone.
evidence: This is stated as established medical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Unilateral fibular deficiency occurs in two-thirds of FH patients.
source: Unilateral fibular deficiency occurs in two-thirds of patients, with the right fibula being more often affected.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In FH patients with unilateral deficiency, the right fibula is more often affected.
source: Unilateral fibular deficiency occurs in two-thirds of patients, with the right fibula being more often affected.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Partial absence of the fibula occurs in 10% of FH cases.
source: FH may vary from partial absence of the fibula (10% of cases) with relatively normal-appearing limbs, to absence of the fibula with marked shortening of the femur, curved tibia, bowing of the leg, knee joint and ankle instability, and significant soft tissue deficiency.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The major functional deficiency in FH results from limb length discrepancy in patients with unilateral FH.
source: The major functional deficiency results from limb length discrepancy in patients with unilateral FH or asymmetrical dwarfism in patients with bilateral FH.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The major functional deficiency in FH results from asymmetrical dwarfism in patients with bilateral FH.
source: The major functional deficiency results from limb length discrepancy in patients with unilateral FH or asymmetrical dwarfism in patients with bilateral FH.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In FH, the foot is generally in an equinovalgus position.
source: The foot is generally in an equinovalgus position.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The extent of FH deformity tends to increase with growth due to limited growing potential within the affected bone.
source: As there is limited growing potential within the affected bone, the extent of the deformity tends to increase with growth.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: FH is occasionally associated with congenital shortening of the femur.
source: Occasionally, FH is associated with congenital shortening of the femur.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: FH was first described by Gollier in 1698.
source: Although it was first described by Gollier in 1698, the etiology of FH remains unknown (Stanitski and Stanitski, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as historical fact with citation.

claim: The etiology of FH remains unknown.
source: Although it was first described by Gollier in 1698, the etiology of FH remains unknown (Stanitski and Stanitski, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The deformity of FH is probably due to disruptions during the critical period of embryonic limb development, between 4th and 7th week of gestation.
source: The deformity of FH is probably due to disruptions during the critical period of embryonic limb development, between 4th and 7th week of gestation.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on established knowledge.

claim: Vascular dysgenesis has been suggested as a possible cause of FH.
source: Vascular dysgenesis, viral infections, trauma, and environmental influences have been suggested as possible causes.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: Viral infections have been suggested as a possible cause of FH.
source: Vascular dysgenesis, viral infections, trauma, and environmental influences have been suggested as possible causes.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: Trauma has been suggested as a possible cause of FH.
source: Vascular dysgenesis, viral infections, trauma, and environmental influences have been suggested as possible causes.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: Environmental influences have been suggested as a possible cause of FH.
source: Vascular dysgenesis, viral infections, trauma, and environmental influences have been suggested as possible causes.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: Most FH cases are sporadic.
source: Most cases are sporadic.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge.

claim: A family history has been reported in a small percentage of FH cases with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and incomplete penetrance.
source: A family history has been reported in a small percentage of cases with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and incomplete penetrance.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge.

claim: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway controls many biological processes during development and maintains tissue homeostasis.
source: The evolutionary conserved canonical Wnt signaling pathway controls many biological processes during the development and maintains tissue homeostasis (Clevers and Nusse, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: A key feature of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway is the regulation of β-catenin by a cytoplasmic destruction complex.
source: A key feature of this pathway is the regulation of its downstream effector β-catenin by a cytoplasmic destruction complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Wnt pathway.

claim: Axin1 is a central scaffold protein of the destruction complex.
source: Axin1 is a central scaffold protein of the destruction complex and directly interacts with all other core components in this complex (Clevers and Nusse, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Axin1 directly interacts with all other core components in the destruction complex.
source: Axin1 is a central scaffold protein of the destruction complex and directly interacts with all other core components in this complex (Clevers and Nusse, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Axin1 is the rate-limiting factor regulating β-catenin signaling.
source: It has been reported that Axin1 is the rate-limiting factor regulating β-catenin signaling (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Axin1 mutant mice exhibit early embryonic lethality at E9.5.
source: However, the in vivo role of Axin1 in the skeletal development and homeostasis has not been fully investigated due to early embryonic lethality (E9.5) of Axin1 mutant mice (Zeng et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling plays a crucial role in controlling craniofacial, limb, and joint formation.
source: Genetic evidence from both humans and mice has implicated that Wnt/β-catenin signaling plays a crucial role in controlling all major aspects of skeletal development, including craniofacial, limb, and joint formation (Baron and Kneissel, 2013; Regard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: BMP signaling plays an important role in skeletogenesis during development.
source: Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling also plays an important role in skeletogenesis during the development (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2006; Yoon et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Wnt and BMP signaling pathways have overlapped functions in controlling skeletal development and homeostasis.
source: Thus, consistent with what is observed in many tissues and organs, Wnt and BMP signaling pathways have overlapped functions in controlling skeletal development and homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on established knowledge.

claim: Loss of Axin1 in mouse limb mesenchymal cells resulted in severe defects in lower limb development, similar to FH disease phenotype.
source: Here, we show that loss of Axin1 in mouse limb mesenchymal cells resulted in severe defects in lower limb development, similar to FH disease phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the introduction.

claim: Deletion of one allele of β-catenin gene in limb mesenchymal cells was able to significantly rescue the defects in FH phenotype observed in Axin1 knockout mice.
source: We found that inhibition of β-catenin signaling, either by deletion of one allele of β-catenin gene in limb mesenchymal cells or by the treatment with a specific β-catenin inhibitor, was able to significantly rescue the defects in FH phenotype observed in Axin1 knockout (KO) mice.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the introduction.

claim: Treatment with a specific β-catenin inhibitor was able to significantly rescue the defects in FH phenotype observed in Axin1 knockout mice.
source: We found that inhibition of β-catenin signaling, either by deletion of one allele of β-catenin gene in limb mesenchymal cells or by the treatment with a specific β-catenin inhibitor, was able to significantly rescue the defects in FH phenotype observed in Axin1 knockout (KO) mice.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the introduction.

claim: Inhibition of BMP signaling significantly reversed defects in limb development and FH phenotype of Axin1 mutant mice.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of BMP signaling also significantly reversed defects in limb development and FH phenotype of Axin1 mutant mice.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding in the introduction.

claim: Axin1/β-catenin/BMP signaling plays a key role in FH development and pathogenesis.
source: Our findings indicate that Axin1/β-catenin/BMP signaling plays a key role in FH development and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the introduction based on the findings.

claim: Axin1 expression was reduced by 61% in joint tissue of 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice.
source: We first determined Axin1 and β-catenin expression in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and found that Axin1 expression was reduced by 61% (Figure 1A, BFigure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—source data 2)
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: β-catenin expression increased 2.8-fold in joint tissue of 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice.
source: in contrast, β-catenin expression increased 2.8-fold in joint tissue (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: The fibulae of Axin1 cKO mice did not mineralize even at P7.
source: The fibulae of Axin1 cKO mice did not mineralize even at P7.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: Axin1 cKO mice showed partially developed fibular tissues with poorly developed growth plate.
source: Histological analysis using limb tissues dissected from Axin1 cKO mice showed partially developed fibular tissues with poorly developed growth plate (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of chondrocytes was significantly reduced in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: The number of chondrocytes was significantly reduced and the structure of growth plate was disorganized in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The structure of growth plate was disorganized in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: The number of chondrocytes was significantly reduced and the structure of growth plate was disorganized in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The lengths of femorae and tibiae were significantly reduced in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: In addition to fibular defects, the lengths of femorae and tibiae were significantly reduced in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—source data 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: High bone mass phenotype was observed in all long bones, including femorae, tibiae, and fibulae in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: High bone mass phenotype was observed in all long bones, including femorae, tibiae, and fibulae in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: 52 Axin1 cKO mice have been analyzed and all of them have a fibular deficiency phenotype.
source: To date, we have analyzed 52 Axin1 cKO mice and all of them have a fibular deficiency phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of experimental observations.

claim: 27 out of 52 Axin1 cKO mice were completely or almost completely absence of fibulae (>50% loss of fibulae).
source: Radiographic analysis of 4- and 8-week-old mice showed that some of Axin1 cKO mice were completely or almost completely absence of fibulae (>50% loss of fibulae, 27/52) where only a distal, vestigial fragment was present.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of radiographic analysis.

claim: 23 out of 52 Axin1 cKO mice had partial absence of the fibulae (30–50% loss of fibulae).
source: The other Axin1 cKO mice had partial absence of the fibulae (30–50% loss of fibulae, 23/52) in which the proximal portions of the fibulae were absent while distal portions were present but could not support the ankle (Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of radiographic analysis with supporting figure.

claim: Mild fibular defects were observed in 2 out of 52 Axin1 cKO mice, in which the fibulae were absent less than 30% of their normal length.
source: The mild fibular defects were observed in few of Axin1 cKO mice (2/52), in which the fibulae were absent less than 30% of their normal length (Figure 2H, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of radiographic analysis with supporting figure.

claim: Axin1 plays an essential role in fibular development.
source: These results demonstrate that Axin1 plays an essential role in fibular development.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: All femorae of Axin1 cKO mice were shorter and wider than those of their Cre- littermates.
source: In addition, all femorae of Axin1 cKO mice were shorter and wider than those of their Cre- littermates (Figure 2H, I, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Axin1 cKO mice always displayed fibular defects in both sides of lower limb.
source: Different from human FH disease, Axin1 cKO mice always displayed fibular defects in both sides of lower limb (Figure 2J, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Bowed tibiae were observed in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: It is also interesting to note that the bowed tibiae were observed in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 2G–J, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: The skeletal defects observed in Axin1 cKO mice have been reported to be the key features of FH disease in humans.
source: These skeletal defects observed in Axin1 cKO mice have been reported to be the key features of FH disease in humans (Achterman and Kalamchi, 1979).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to human disease with citation.

claim: Deletion of Axin1 in Sox9-expressing cells does not affect fibular development.
source: In contrast to Axin1 cKO mice, deletion of Axin1 in Sox9-, Col2a1-, and Sp7-expressing cells does not affect fibular development (Figure 2K, Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Deletion of Axin1 in Col2a1-expressing cells does not affect fibular development.
source: In contrast to Axin1 cKO mice, deletion of Axin1 in Sox9-, Col2a1-, and Sp7-expressing cells does not affect fibular development (Figure 2K, Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Deletion of Axin1 in Sp7-expressing cells does not affect fibular development.
source: In contrast to Axin1 cKO mice, deletion of Axin1 in Sox9-, Col2a1-, and Sp7-expressing cells does not affect fibular development (Figure 2K, Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: FH disease is caused by defects in the specific cell population, limb mesenchymal cells.
source: suggesting that FH disease is caused by defects in the specific cell population, limb mesenchymal cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the cell-type specific deletion experiments.

claim: Axin1 cKO mice had dysplasia of acetabulum.
source: The dysplasia of acetabulum and defects in femoral head development were found by microcomputed tomography (μCT) analysis in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Axin1 cKO mice had defects in femoral head development.
source: The dysplasia of acetabulum and defects in femoral head development were found by microcomputed tomography (μCT) analysis in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Hypoplasia of knee joint was found in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice.
source: We performed X-ray and μCT analyses on knee joint and found hypoplasia of knee joint in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Tarsal coalition phenotype was found in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: The tarsal coalition phenotype was also found in Axin1 cKO mice and distal tarsals 2, 3, and 4 were fused together (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Distal tarsals 2, 3, and 4 were fused together in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: The tarsal coalition phenotype was also found in Axin1 cKO mice and distal tarsals 2, 3, and 4 were fused together (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling regulates osteoclast formation.
source: It is known that Wnt/β-catenin signaling regulates osteoclast formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: There was a significant decrease in osteoclast formation in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: We then performed TRAP staining and examined changes in TRAP-positive osteoclast numbers in Axin1 cKO mice and found a significant decrease in osteoclast formation in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 3E, F, Figure 3—source data 1–2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Inhibition of osteoclast formation may contribute to the high bone mass phenotype observed in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: Inhibition of osteoclast formation may contribute to the high bone mass phenotype observed in Axin1 cKO mice.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the osteoclast data.

claim: Expression of VEGF was significantly reduced in joint tissues of 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice.
source: We also performed immunofluorescent (IF) staining of VEGF and found that expression of VEGF was significantly reduced in joint tissues of 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 3G, H, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Reduced VEGF expression may be related to the hypoplasia phenotype of lower limb in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: Reduced VEGF expression may be related to the hypoplasia phenotype of lower limb in Axin1 cKO mice.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the VEGF data.

claim: Deletion of Axin1 elevated β-catenin protein levels.
source: Since Axin1 is a well-known negative regulator of canonical Wnt pathway, deletion of Axin1 elevated β-catenin protein levels.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on established knowledge and experimental data.

claim: Deletion of one allele of the β-catenin gene under Axin1 cKO background significantly reversed defects in fibular development.
source: We found that deletion of one allele of the β-catenin gene under Axin1 cKO background significantly reversed defects in fibular development (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—source data 1)
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Deletion of one allele of the β-catenin gene caused reduction of BV from 92% to 71% in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: and caused reduction of BV from 92% to 71% (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: iCRT14 specifically inhibits β-catenin-induced transcription by disrupting the interaction between β-catenin and TCF4.
source: It has been shown that iCRT14 specifically inhibits β-catenin-induced transcription by disrupting the interaction between β-catenin and TCF4 (Gonsalves et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Treatment with iCRT14 rescued the fibular defect phenotype in Axin1 cKO embryos.
source: Histological analysis showed that the fibular defect phenotype in Axin1 cKO embryos were rescued by the treatment with iCRT14 (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Treatment with iCRT14 rescued fibular defects in 4-week-old Axin1 cKO mice.
source: The rescuing of fibular defects with iCRT14 treatment was also confirmed by μCT analysis in 4-week-old Axin1 cKO mice receiving iCRT14 treatment (Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt secretion with LGK974 did not rescue the fibular defects observed in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: It is interesting to note that inhibition of Wnt secretion with LGK974 did not rescue the fibular defects observed in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: LGK974 is a specific small molecule compound of porcupine inhibitor, which inhibits Wnt secretion in vitro and in vivo.
source: LGK974 is a specific small molecule compound of porcupine inhibitor, which inhibits Wnt secretion in vitro and in vivo (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Axin1 controls the fibular development through the canonical β-catenin signaling pathway.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that Axin1 controls the fibular development through the canonical β-catenin signaling pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the genetic and pharmacological rescue experiments.

claim: Bmp2 expression was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos.
source: We found that expression of Bmp2, Bmp4, Gremlin1, and Msx2 was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos (Figure 5A–E, Figure 5—source data 1–5).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Bmp4 expression was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos.
source: We found that expression of Bmp2, Bmp4, Gremlin1, and Msx2 was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos (Figure 5A–E, Figure 5—source data 1–5).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Gremlin1 expression was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos.
source: We found that expression of Bmp2, Bmp4, Gremlin1, and Msx2 was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos (Figure 5A–E, Figure 5—source data 1–5).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Msx2 expression was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos.
source: We found that expression of Bmp2, Bmp4, Gremlin1, and Msx2 was significantly upregulated in limb tissues of Axin1 cKO embryos (Figure 5A–E, Figure 5—source data 1–5).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Dorsomorphin inhibits BMPR-IA (ALK3), BMPR-IB (ALK6), and ALK2 activity.
source: Dorsomorphin has been shown to inhibit BMPR-IA (ALK3), BMPR-IB (ALK6), and ALK2 activity (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Fibular defects in Axin1 cKO embryos were significantly rescued by the treatment with dorsomorphin.
source: Analysis of histological sections of hindlimbs of E18.5 embryos showed that fibular defects in Axin1 cKO embryos were significantly rescued by the treatment with dorsomorphin (Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: The fibular defect phenotype observed in Axin1 cKO mice was significantly reversed by the treatment with dorsomorphin.
source: The result of μCT analysis of 6-week-old mice confirmed that the fibular defect phenotype observed in Axin1 cKO mice was significantly reversed by the treatment with dorsomorphin (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Single dose of BMP inhibitor was not able to reverse high bone mass phenotype caused by continuing upregulation of BMP signaling in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: In contrast, single dose of BMP inhibitor (2.5 mg/kg at E9.5 stage) was not able to reverse high bone mass phenotype caused by continuing upregulation of BMP signaling in Axin1 cKO mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Dorsomorphin did not affect fibular development in the Cre- control mice.
source: Also, dorsomorphin did not affect fibular development in the Cre- control mice (Figure 5F, G, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Dorsomorphin lost its protective effect if injected after embryonic E12.5 stage.
source: We also determined the stage-specific effect of dorsomorphin on reversing fibular defects in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice and found that dorsomorphin lost its protective effect if injected after embryonic E12.5 stage (Figure 5H, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Administration of dorsomorphin at E12.5 stage significantly reversed fibular defects in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice.
source: Administration of dorsomorphin at E12.5 stage significantly reversed fibular defects as well as rescuing knee join dysplasia phenotype in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 5I, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Administration of dorsomorphin at E12.5 stage rescued knee joint dysplasia phenotype in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice.
source: Administration of dorsomorphin at E12.5 stage significantly reversed fibular defects as well as rescuing knee join dysplasia phenotype in 3-week-old Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 5I, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: TGF-β inhibitor SB-505124 had no effect on reversing fibular defect in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: In contrast, same concentration of TGF-β inhibitor, small chemical compound SB-505124, had no effect on reversing fibular defect in Axin1 cKO mice (Figure 5J, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: BMP signaling upregulation contributes to the FH defects observed in Axin1 cKO mice.
source: These results demonstrate that BMP signaling upregulation also contributes to the FH defects observed in Axin1 cKO mice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the BMP inhibition experiments.

claim: Endogenous Axin1 interacted with Smad5 in C3H10T1/2 cells.
source: The results of co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays revealed that endogenous Axin1 indeed interacted with Smad5 in C3H10T1/2 cells (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: The pSmad5 levels decreased gradually after removal of BMP2 in Cre- cells.
source: The pSmad5 levels decreased gradually after removal of BMP2 in Cre- cells, but duration of pSmad5 was much longer in Axin1 mutant cells (Figure 6B, C, Figure 6—source data 2–3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Duration of pSmad5 was much longer in Axin1 mutant cells compared to Cre- cells.
source: The pSmad5 levels decreased gradually after removal of BMP2 in Cre- cells, but duration of pSmad5 was much longer in Axin1 mutant cells (Figure 6B, C, Figure 6—source data 2–3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figures.

claim: Axin1 could inhibit BMP signaling through promoting pSmad5 degradation.
source: The results indicate that Axin1 could also inhibit BMP signaling through promoting pSmad5 degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the pulse-chase experiments.

claim: Treatment with iCRT14 did not affect the duration of pSmad5 in Cre- cells.
source: The treatment with iCRT14 did not affect the duration of pSmad5 in Cre- cells as well as in Axin1-deficient cells (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Treatment with iCRT14 did not affect the duration of pSmad5 in Axin1-deficient cells.
source: The treatment with iCRT14 did not affect the duration of pSmad5 in Cre- cells as well as in Axin1-deficient cells (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: LGK974 blocked the Wnt3a-induced prolonged duration of pSmad5.
source: In contrast, LGK974 did block the Wnt3a-induced prolonged duration of pSmad5 (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting figure.

claim: Axin1 regulated pSmad5 levels are independent from β-catenin.
source: These results suggest that Axin1 regulated pSmad5 levels are independent from β-catenin.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the iCRT14 and LGK974 experiments.

claim: Wnt3a significantly prolonged the duration of the pSmad5 at the similar extent as the treatment with proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: Indeed, Wnt3a significantly prolonged the duration of the pSmad5 at the similar extent as the treatment with proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 5–6)
